Journalists always ask me the same question, and it is the one question I will not answer. Which country is better. There is no such measurement and there never was.
Although you do produce a ranking. Eleventh on one index, forty-second on another — somebody has to explain that.
And I will, gladly. The two indices measure different things, they weight them differently, and one of them is per capita and the other is not. That is the whole mystery.
So the more you look at the two lists, the less either of them means?
The more you look, the more you learn — about the people who built the index. Every ranking is an argument about what matters, expressed as arithmetic.
That is a sentence I would put on a wall. What would you tell somebody who just wants an answer?
Ask what the yardstick is, and ask whether it is like for like. Two questions, and about half the comparisons in the newspaper do not survive them.
And the other half? Because I would not want to end up refusing to compare anything at all.
What is the yardstick, and is it like for like?
In relative terms it is enormous, and in absolute terms it is small.
It is nowhere near as clear as the ranking makes it look.
Every ranking is an argument about what matters, expressed as arithmetic.

The example I use with students is a country whose economy doubled overnight. Not over a decade. Overnight, in the sense that on one day the published figure was one number and on the following day it was roughly twice that. Nothing whatever had changed in the country. What changed was the base year. The statistics had been calculated against a structure of the economy from decades earlier, and when the base year was finally updated, whole sectors that had grown enormously appeared in the accounts for the first time. Now, that country did not become richer. It became better measured. And every international ranking that included it had, until that morning, been comparing a modern measurement in one country with a very old one in another. That is the thing to hold on to: international rankings compare measurements, and measurements are not countries.

I want to defend the rankings, and I will start where my critics are strongest. The weighting is a value judgement. When an index decides that one indicator counts for thirty per cent and another for five, somebody has made a moral choice and dressed it as arithmetic, and it is almost never explained. Granted. Here is my problem with the criticism. If we conclude from that that no comparison is possible, we have not achieved neutrality. We have simply left the field to worse comparisons, made by people with fewer scruples and larger platforms. The answer is not to stop ranking. It is to publish the weighting alongside the ranking, in the same document, in the same size of type, so that the argument becomes an argument about the weighting. That is a conversation we can actually have.
